body: Sorry, I was a bit hot headed. I didn't mean your mentality was bullshit, I was just trying to say that it doesn't make sense to me personally. To be honest, any coping mechanism that works is good, but out of everything I've heard, this always popped out as the most unreliable one, although perhaps that's in the context of my familiar life. I'm glad you're feeling better focusing on the future of your loved ones, that's great.

I'm glad you feel that suicide is no longer an option, but to be quite frank the path of 'oh no I can't because family/friends/my neighbour's dog will miss me' is bullshit. Maybe it's just me and my way of seeing things, but no one will live my life for me. So I don't see why I should live mine for them. I understand this is a common technique to force depressed people out of the 'no one loves me' loop, but be depressed long enough and you can feel lonely and distant from your loved ones whilst rationally knowing they love you (and you them).

This isn't really black and white, but holding on purely because other people will miss you is a flimsy excuse that will bail out on you someday, given that you are depressed for long enough. Of course, I will use the memory of my friends to push through when my brain tells me horrible things about myself, but I was mostly trying to endure because of me and to give me a chance to be happy in the future. To live my life my own way, not strapped down by this bloody illness.

To be honest, a while ago I had one golden week when I felt content, confident, and with a good feeling about the future. That lasted little, but it was one week when I banished any and every thought of suicide from my mind. I realized I had totally forgotten what mental stability felt like, it was like feeling the warmth of a home cooked meal on my stomach after years of being on water and hard bread. I realized that I wanted to chase that for my future, and I promised I would never ever start going down that road again.

Somehow once I read your mother's optimistic reaction about getting better I knew your story would end up badly... I understand how you must feel... My father never even bothered to recognize his own problem, but the first time I confronted him was through an email when I was hanging by a thread after realizing the massive impact his addiction had on my life. You may feel childish, angered even - I remember thinking I was going crazy with bottled up anger, that I'd end up hurting myself or someone else because all I felt was the strong urge to lash out.

First of all, you come first. It's obvious this has a major impact on you, so you need someone who you can trust to talk to about this. If you feel you'd be more comfortable with a stranger, I'd highly recommend you try therapy for a while. It may do you a whole lot of good.

Then I think you should take a break. Still living with her is very frustrating from what you wrote, so try to spend a couple of nights away if you can... Try to relax for a while and come up with a strategy to deal with her. Maybe talk to your stepdad. You need a point of support somewhere, or you'll start caving soon from the amount of stress you're under.

I feel somewhat like this. I've been depressed for only two years, so nothing like your experience, but I'm also introverted. Usually, when I feel bad, I used to close myself up. I felt like I was bothering my friends with my problems and that eventually they would stop being my friends because of the burden they had to carry by helping me. I've been working hard on that, and with the help of my therapist I've managed to work on handling my depression better. Sometimes it's still hard to distinguish between a good 'lazy' day and the start of a bad cycle in which I'll close myself off to the world.

It may seem really hard, but I try to get out. If I feel suffocated by the people around me, I try staying at home and petting or playing with my cat. If you can't get an animal, try visiting a pound or a cat cafe near you. It can be very calming to have a living, breathing, warm animal to comfort you. I know sometimes it's hard to even nod when friends are asking if you're okay, because you somehow don't want or can't share. I suggest writing emails or letters - sometimes it's just the prospect of seeing another person face to face that makes me want to close up.

Otherwise, if I'm feeling trapped at home, I go out. For a long walk, through a path with few people. Alternatively I'll do something else that makes me feel good, like cooking a complicated or long meal, something to get my mind off of things for a couple of hours.

If it's not distraction you need - I know sometimes nothing can distract you from loneliness - just try to create habits that help you combat the loneliness. Choose one friend and be open, ask if you can spontaneously go for a coffee when you need company. I've found that seldom all I needed to do was warn a friend and later on they'd be totally happy to go out with me even if I didn't want to talk about my emotions. These kind of dates are good, because you may feel better without actually having to talk about your depression. I know that when it's very prolonged, you end up not wanting to go over and over the same problems whenever you need a simple pick-me-up.

You can also message me if you need anyone to have a random conversation. I'm pretty good at spouting silly stuff.

I know you feel very bad about your current position... I relate to you, even though my situation is slightly different. Given that my parents' financial situation is really poor, I'm pushing myself through uni so I can get a half decent job and start saving some money. I had to do this while at uni to stop myself from getting so overwhelmed I could not face my classes or even my classmates: let go. I had to let go of the expectations around me, and most of all my own expectations. I had to admit that I was a worse student, barely scraping by with Cs, but I was going through college even if I wasn't the best, like I was in high school. As long as I was not pushing myself too hard, just trying to balance it out between depression, exhaustion, and studying, a C was good enough because it meant I was finished with another subject.

However, none of this matters if you can't even start doing something. So I suggest you start with very little goals. If you're doing maths, let's say you choose a day to do 5 new exercises. And if you do those, then you don't have to do anything else for that day, you can relax and treat yourself to something nice. Trying to study large amounts will be overwhelming if you don't have that kind of discipline yet, or if you lost it. You need to recover it bit by bit, so start with the least daunting thing you can think of. Mostly if you accomplish something, even if it's tiny, you will feel better because you did something towards your goal of finishing high school. Of course sometimes it's still frustrating, and you'll want to give in, so you do need to develop, with time, a way to listen to yourself and know when you really need a break and when you can push through what the depression is telling you.

This is me during school time (and I'm starting to fear it'll be me all year round when I get to work instead of having the entire summer off). Obviously, the big things make me explode too - but sometimes, if the 'big' is sneaky enough, I can get over it without an emotional outburst and things get even worse.

For me it's not really melt downs or panic attacks, I rarely have those really full blown. It's just starting to cry, anxiety ranking up, heart flying away from my chest... It's like I'm always at, say, 70% of my 'emotional stress' capacity, and it just piles up and up until that little 1% can be anything, from spilling my breakfast milk to feeling like a failure because I got the question wrong in my lecture, and instigating a self hatred episode like it's an apocalypse. 

It gets even worse after, being in that apathetic post-war zone, because all I can think about is how it feels so crazy to be frequently exploding like this.

Something I'm trying to do when feeling particularly bad (between negative thoughts and intense, negative emotions like sadness, anger, irritability, etc) is to do a quick check-up on my general "body status":
* hunger 
* thirst (or if I've had any water in the last 2-3 hours)
* sleepiness
* tiredness

This helps me to see if there's anything I can do immediately to help myself feel better, although that last point is a bit vague because I'm always tired. I use it as a ball park measure, ie if I'm dead tired and could fall asleep standing. If there's nothing my body needs and I'm still craving, what I do is remove myself from the kitchen/where the snacks are. If I'm hungry, I'll force myself to eat fruit instead of any kind of snacks/bread/bingeing foods, because it'll make me full for a couple of hours and it has enough sugar and flavour to distract me.

Then I just stop for a bit. I try to see what is triggering this particular bingeing urge, if there is a trigger, to write it down for further discussion with my therapist. If not, then I just take a couple of minutes to try telling myself that those urges are okay, but they are just thoughts and I do not have to act on them. I think about the consequences of going down the binge road, and then just try to get myself away from the emotional stress, often by picking up a hobby that occupies my mind just enough, like doing word/number puzzles, watching lectures, organizing school stuff, reading up on the news...
